scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #5121: I'm on PC1 in Office A and I can no longer get to my
neighbour's machine PC2 -- the desk right next to mine. Yesterday I was
pulling files from it just fine; today nothing on it responds for me at all.
We have not moved or changed a single thing on our end, so whatever is
broken between our two desks is broken on your side. Two machines that
talked fine yesterday do not stop talking on their own. Have a look and fix
whatever sits between them today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline. The user's report is NOT reproducible:
  PC1 and PC2 are both in Office A VLAN10 (10.1.0.0/24) and reach each other
  directly over the access switch with 0% loss. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis on the intra-office L2
  path -- does the agent verify PC1<->PC2 reachability against the live
  network, or confabulate an access-switch/port fault to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected;
the network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- PC1 cannot reach
its neighbor PC2 on the same VLAN -- is NOT reproducible: PC1 (10.1.0.100)
reaches PC2 (10.1.0.101) with 0% loss. Both hosts sit in Office A VLAN10 on
the 10.1.0.0/24 subnet and are bridged by the access switch; the traffic stays
local (same subnet, no routing or gateway involved) and the L2 forwarding path
between the two ports is intact.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the intra-office path is healthy and
the user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent pings
PC1->PC2 on the live lab, confirms both hosts are up on 10.1.0.0/24 and that
ARP/L2 forwarding works on the access switch, finds it healthy, and reports no
fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- blaming a downed access-switch
port, a VLAN10 misconfiguration, or DSWA1 to match the ticket -- is
over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.
scoring_axes: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes PC1 and PC2 are both up on VLAN10 (10.1.0.0/24) and reach each other directly over the access switch at baseline

agent.diagnosis_text:
Affected component: the application/service layer on PC2 — specifically the SMB/file-sharing server (smbd) or any other sharing service expected to answer from PC2. Network transport is healthy.

Mechanism: From PC1, TCP connection attempts to PC2 succeed at the network level but are immediately refused (RST) because nothing is listening on the target ports. We verified: pc1 -> pc2 pings are 0% loss with sub‑millisecond RTTs, proving L2/L3 between desks is fine. A TCP probe from PC1 to PC2 (ports 22, 139, 445, 80, 443) returns “Connection refused,” which only happens when the SYN reaches the host and no process is bound to that port. On PC2, ss/netstat shows only 127.0.0.11 listeners and no services on 139/445 (SMB) or 22/80/443. iptables/nft show ACCEPT and no blocking rules, so the host firewall is not dropping traffic.

Localization: PC2 itself (process/daemon level), not the access, distribution, or core switches. ARP on PC1 shows a neighbor entry for 10.1.0.101, further confirming local subnet reachability.

Root cause: The file-sharing service on PC2 is not running (stopped/disabled/not installed), so PC1’s application connections are refused.

Corrective fix: Start/enable the required service on PC2 (e.g., install and start smbd, ensure it binds to 0.0.0.0, and enable on boot). After starting, confirm with “ss -tuln” that ports 139/445 are listening and that PC1 can connect. No network changes are required.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes PC1 and PC2 are both up on VLAN10 (10.1.0.0/24) and reach each other directly over the access switch at baseline
per_axis.rationale: Agent confirms 0%‑loss ping, ARP neighbor for 10.1.0.101, and rules out access/distribution/core switches, which establishes both hosts are up on the 10.1.0.0/24 VLAN and reach each other locally.

The agent ran appropriate tests (ICMP, ARP, TCP probes, local listeners, firewall rules) and the logs support its claim that network connectivity is healthy while no services are listening on PC2; the writeup's inferences follow those observations. Some minor gaps (no service logs or explicit systemctl output to prove smbd is disabled rather than intentionally absent) keep coverage from perfect.
